```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

## BSSD for a blinded ongoing study
Having specified a prior for the adverse event rate under placebo (see [Article 1 - Specifying priors](article-1-priors.html)), let us now concern ourselves with analysing data in an exchangeable (i.e. scientifically similar) ongoing study.

We will conduct an interim analysis after 100 patients have been followed-up where these patients are randomized 2:1 (i.e. 1/3 in the placebo arm (arm 1) and 2/3 in the active arm (arm 2)).
To simulate some outcomes, let's assume that the hazard of event is 10% under placebo and 20% under active:

```{r}
set.seed(2024)
prob_arm1 <- 1 / 3
N <- 100
time <- 0.5 + cumsum(rexp(N, 100))
arm <- sample(1:2, size = N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(prob_arm1, 1 - prob_arm1))
hazard1 <- 0.1
hazard2 <- 0.2
prob <- numeric(length = N)
prob[arm == 1] <- 1 - exp(- hazard1 * time[arm == 1])
prob[arm == 2] <- 1 - exp(- hazard2 * time[arm == 2])
y <- rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = prob)
```

Let's summarise our interim data:
```{r}
library(dplyr)
summary_df <- tibble(arm, y, time, prob) %>%
  group_by(arm) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_prob = mean(prob),
    events = sum(y),
    n = n(),
    event_rate = mean(y),
    mean_tar = mean(time),
    .groups = "drop")
summary_df
```

We will use the following MAP prior derived using patient-level data from relevant historical studies for the placebo arm. See this link: [Patient-level MAP prior](./article-1-priors.html#map-prior) for a refresher on how derive MAP priors using patient-level data.

```{r}
w1 <- c(0.556, 0.444)
pi1_alpha <- c(6.673, 4.614)
pi1_beta <- c(27.393, 25.853)
```

We will also use a $Beta(1/3, 1/3)$ prior on the active arm, reflecting our relative ignorance:

```{r}
w2 <- 1
pi2_alpha <- 1 / 3
pi2_beta <- 1 / 3
```


#### Blinded ongoing study
To fit the BSSD model for blinded outcomes, we call `stan_bssd` and specify the `prob_arm1` parameter:

```{r, cache=TRUE}
fit <- stan_bssd(y = y, time = time, prob_arm1 = prob_arm1,
                 w1 = w1, pi1_alpha = pi1_alpha, pi1_beta = pi1_beta,
                 w2 = w2, pi2_alpha = pi2_alpha, pi2_beta = pi2_beta,
                 refresh = 0, seed = 2024)
```

We obtain the estimated mean event rate in each arm, and the posterior probability that the true event rate is greater in the active arm:

```{r}
fit
```

The model is `r round(summary(fit)$mean[summary(fit)$variable == "prob_higher"], 3)` sure that the true event rate is greater under active arm.

We can obtain summary statistics of the result data:

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

We can also extract a specific value from the fit `summary()` function, e.g., the mean for `pi1` from the previous table:
```{r}
summary(fit)$mean[summary(fit)$variable == "pi1"]
```

As before, we have default methods for visualising the model inferences:

```{r}
plot(fit)
```

and naturally further analysis is possible using the MCMC samples contained within the `fit` object, along with the various methods designed for Stan model fits.
For instance, a traceplot is easily obtained:

```{r}
rstan::traceplot(fit$fit)
```
